segments.content:
Chapter 223 0220 When Can China's GDP Rank Second?

Dean Wu personally acted as the host: "Everyone, why do you think venture capital has been so crazy this year?"

"Who would like to start?"

The several alumni looked at each other.

"Let's take turns."

"President Wang is our senior, so President Wang should go first."

Wang Zhidong took the microphone: "When doing anything in China, you must first look at the policy environment. By the end of last year, the split-share structure reform was basically complete. It's been nearly two years since the Shenzhen Stock Exchange established the SME board, and its subsequent effects have become fully apparent. The policy-level support for venture capital is becoming clearer by the day. These factors have allowed VC firms to set aside their worries."

"That's the policy environment. Then there's the industry environment. The 2000 internet bubble terrified global capital. After a few years of recovery, it finally bounced back, and a large amount of venture capital has been invested in an almost retaliatory fashion."

Wang Zhidong only briefly covered one part, deliberately not giving the full answer.

Li Guoqin continued: "The successive IPOs of Chinese companies represented by Baidu, Shanda, and Focus Media allowed VC firms to successfully exit their prior investments. And they all made a huge profit. Taking just a small portion of that money to reinvest is enough to seem crazy."

"Indeed," said Lei Ming, "Venture capital is for making money. The hotter the investment climate, the easier it is to exit, and the more firms will enter the market. Now, even several local RMB funds have emerged."

Wang Zhidong commented: "Local firms are still relatively conservative at present, mainly investing in mature companies, traditional enterprises, and tech companies about to go public. It would be delightful if one day, local firms dared to invest in tech startups."

Chen Guiliang followed up: "There's another important reason, which is China's high-speed economic growth and the increasing popularity of the internet. One-ninth of the world's netizens are in China, so it's only natural for venture capital to flock here."

Everyone was being very polite, each speaking only one segment.

Dean Wu asked: "How long do you think this situation will last?"

"At least a year," Wang Zhidong said.

Chen Guiliang said: "In the coming year, it will get crazier and crazier. As more VC firms enter the market, the competition for projects will become more intense. I estimate that soon they won't even need to do detailed due diligence, and they'll also substantially raise valuations, departing from basic business logic and financial models. A lot of startups will die!"

"Why will a lot of startups die?" asked Wu Minhui, who hadn't said much.

Chen Guiliang said: "When VC firms don't follow business logic, some entrepreneurs will certainly cater to their preferences. They'll do whatever project is hot, all for the sake of rapid financing, rather than focusing their energy on building products and businesses. When the VC craze subsides, these companies won't be far from death."

Wang Zhidong nodded: "That's certainly true. A large number of such companies will definitely emerge this year."

Li Guoqin picked up the microphone: "So, if the teachers and students present here want to start a business, you should still focus on building products and services. Don't just blindly cater to the preferences of VC firms. The hotter the project, the fiercer the competition. Without a core product, you'll die a miserable death!"

Dean Wu said to the teachers and students in attendance: "This is some advice from our alumni. I hope everyone can take it to heart..."

After another twenty minutes of discussion, the Q&A session with the audience began.

The first to ask a question was a graduate student from the Guanghua School of Management: "Last month, Google officially entered China, and Baidu is facing a huge challenge. There have been many similar incidents in recent years, such as the competition between QQ and MSN, and between Dangdang and Joyo Amazon. Also, Cyworld entered China last year, so Kaixin001 is also facing pressure. How should Chinese companies respond to strong foreign rivals?"

Li Guoqin answered: "Dangdang has never considered Amazon a strong rival. Joyo Amazon even needs to apply for approval layer by layer from Amazon's headquarters just to modify its shopping pages. What kind of competitiveness can such a rigid management system have?"

Chen Guiliang laughed: "Cyworld is pretty much the same. I heard they even need to report to their Korean headquarters for approval just to change a button on their website. If you ask me to use Cyworld, I'd rather go play on QQ Qzone. Cyworld's free items are like junk, and anything slightly nice costs money, with a set of virtual clothes starting at 10 yuan. If you don't top up, the user avatars on Cyworld all look like beggars."

Despite him saying that, Cyworld's user base was continuously and rapidly growing.

Its main user group was the "Hallyu fans."

From time to time, Cyworld would invite Korean stars for promotions, which was endlessly attractive to young Hallyu fans. In the eyes of Hallyu fans, Korean stars were untouchable beings, so the fact that Cyworld could invite them made it the most premium and high-class website.

In addition, Cyworld also collaborated with Li Yuchun, which probably attracted tens of thousands of "Corns" to register.

But if you didn't pay, you were treated like dirt. The user experience for free users was abysmal!

The graduate student followed up: "Both of your views are surprisingly consistent, yet MSN's market share is getting higher and higher. According to report data from iResearch, MSN's market share had already reached 23% by the end of last year. If this trend continues, MSN will surpass QQ sooner or later."

MSN's promotional campaign last year was indeed terrifying, and it had established its "reputation" and a "chain of contempt." Its 23% market share put immense pressure on Tencent.

There's a song coming out next year called "Siqingaoli's Sadness," which has two lines that vividly reflect this chain of contempt: Got on QQ to make friends, only to find they're all lovers; I hear the good people often use MSN.

See? The good people are all using MSN...

The several people on stage fell silent.

As high-end individuals, most of them had been using MSN last year. But the user experience was truly terrible, and some had already abandoned it.

Chen Guiliang said: "Take another look at the iResearch report next January. I'm sure there will be a surprise."

What surprise?

MSN's market share in China would plummet from 23% to 10% in just one year!

"Okay, I will continue to follow it." The graduate student did not press further.

Another student asked: "Senior Wang, what do you think of Sina entering the blog market?"

Wang Zhidong's expression soured slightly: "I haven't been paying attention to Sina for a long time."

Chen Guiliang took the opportunity to say: "President Wang will soon be joining Hainei.com... which is Kaixin001."

That student simply asked Chen Guiliang instead: "Hainei.com's journal function is similar to a blog, but it seems that its posts don't get as much attention as blog articles. President Chen, do you think the two are in competition?"

"For now, there isn't much of a competitive relationship. We are, after all, an SNS website."

Chen Guiliang explained in detail: "The popular journals on Kaixin001 are divided into two lists: real-name and anonymous. Those with real-name verification are all celebrities, and they naturally possess buzz and draw attention. The anonymous list, on the other hand, consists of ordinary users. They represent the grassroots power, which the website values and promotes just as heavily."

"In comparison, blog posts by celebrities get a lot of attention, but blogs by ordinary users get extremely little. Even if Sina's blog service shows a trend of developing towards SNS, the interactivity between its users is still too poor."

"Thank you," the student said and sat down.

Another student stood up: "President Chen, that six-locked bicycle of yours, shouldn't it be time to upgrade to a BMW?"

"Hahaha!"

The whole audience burst into laughter.

Even Dean Wu started laughing.

Because Chen Guiliang putting six locks on his shabby bicycle had already become a famous sight on the Peking University campus.

Chen Guiliang retorted: "If I switched to a BMW, where would I park it at night? The suitable parking spots are farther than the walk to my classroom." With that, Chen Guiliang said to Dean Wu, "Professor Wu, I suggest the university builds an underground parking garage near the dormitories."

Dean Wu said with a straight face: "That's not under my purview. You can write a letter to President Xu."

The audience laughed again.

The next person to ask a question also called on Chen Guiliang: "President Chen, how do you balance starting a business and your studies?"

Chen Guiliang shook his head: "I can't balance them. When I first started, I had two companies in my hands and also had to write books for royalties to support them. I was a freshman back then and didn't dare to skip classes wantonly. I was so busy every day that I'd fall asleep the moment I lay down. Right now, I'm just hoping I don't fail too many courses."

Another student asked a question: "In the year 2000, China's GDP ranked sixth in the world. Last year, it finally ranked fifth. In the opinion of our guests, how many more years of development will China need to rank fourth?"

"It should be very soon," Li Guoqin said.

Wang Zhidong said: "I think it will take another two years of development."

The others shook their heads; they hadn't really paid much attention to this.

Chen Guiliang, once again saying something shocking, chimed in: "It will be fourth this year, third next year. By 2010, China's GDP should be able to rank second."

"Hahaha!"

The whole audience erupted in laughter, and it was loud laughter.
